entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To spend free time relaxing somewhere or with someone, without any special plan or activity.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and texts, and fine with coworkers. The patterns are *hang out with* + person and *hang out at* + place; *a hangout* is a place where people often go. Plain *hang* (*Want to hang?*) is slangier and sounds younger.
examples: We used to **hang out** at the diner after school and talk for hours.
My brother and I don't **hang out** much anymore since he moved to Denver.
A few of us from work are **hanging out** at Jen's place on Friday if you want to come.

drill.sentence: "What did you do this weekend?" "Nothing special, just {{hung out}} with some friends at the lake."
drill.hint: relaxed together with no real plan (phrasal verb; not *chilled*)

mistake.wrong: We hanged out at the mall all afternoon.
mistake.right: We hung out at the mall all afternoon.
mistake.why: The past of *hang out* is *hung out*; *hanged* is only used for killing someone by hanging.

entries.related: *chill (out)* — relax, slangier; *hang around* — stay somewhere with nothing much to do; *get together* — meet, usually planned.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Things in general, when you don't need or want to name them exactly: objects, belongings, tasks or topics.
entries.usage: Used constantly in casual speech by all ages and fine in relaxed work talk: *a lot of stuff*, *my stuff*. It is uncountable, so never *stuffs* or *a stuff*; *and stuff* at the end of a list means *and similar things*. In formal writing use *things*, *items*, *belongings* or *material*.
examples: Can you move your **stuff** off the couch? Our guests will be here in ten minutes.
I have a ton of **stuff** to do before my flight tomorrow.
My dad and I don't talk about personal **stuff**; it's mostly sports and the weather.

drill.sentence: I'm moving next month, so I'm selling a lot of my old {{stuff}} online.
drill.hint: what I own, in general (vague uncountable noun; not *things*, *belongings* or *junk*)

mistake.wrong: I bought many stuffs for the new apartment.
mistake.right: I bought a lot of stuff for the new apartment.
mistake.why: *Stuff* is uncountable: use *a lot of*, *some* or *much*, and no plural *-s*.

entries.related: *things* — countable, neutral; *junk* — stuff you think is worthless; *gear* — equipment for an activity (*camping gear*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Really great or very good. *Awesome!* on its own is also a quick reply meaning *great, thanks* or *sounds good*.
entries.usage: Extremely common in American speech, texts and even quick work emails (*Awesome, thanks!*), used by all ages. Americans use it for small everyday things, so it is much weaker than the old sense *causing awe*. Some people find it overused; in formal writing use *excellent* or *impressive*.
examples: We had an **awesome** time at the beach; the water was perfect and nobody got sunburned.
"I'll pick you up at seven." "**Awesome**, see you then!"
Got the slides, thanks! **Awesome** job on the charts.

drill.sentence: "Your package came this morning, so I left it by your door." "{{Awesome}}, thank you so much!"
drill.hint: a happy one-word reply, very common in the US (not *great*, *amazing*, *perfect*, *cool* or *sweet*)

entries.related: *great* — neutral; *amazing* — similar, a little stronger; *cool* — calmer approval, also very common.

entries.label: pronoun
entries.meaning: A casual plural *you*, used to talk to two or more people of any gender.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and in casual messages to a group (*Thanks, you guys!*), and many women use it for groups of women. Some people prefer neutral options such as *you all*, *y'all* (Southern US) or *everyone*, especially when speaking to customers or in formal settings. *Hey guys* is the usual greeting form.
examples: Are **you guys** ready to order, or do you need a few more minutes?
Mom, Dad, I'm so glad **you guys** could make it to my graduation.
Thanks for covering my shift yesterday; **you guys** are lifesavers.

drill.sentence: Hey everyone, are {{you guys}} coming to the barbecue on Saturday, or should I tell Mark you're busy?
drill.hint: plural *you*, casual American (not *y'all* or *you all*)

entries.related: *y'all* — the Southern US plural *you*; *you all* — more neutral; *folks* — friendly, a bit old-fashioned (*Hi, folks!*).

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Completely. In casual American speech, *Totally!* on its own also means *Yes, I completely agree.*
entries.usage: The sense *completely* is standard and fine anywhere (*totally different*). The agreeing reply (*Totally.*) and the use before verbs for emphasis (*I totally forgot*) are casual and sound young or relaxed, so keep them for friends and friendly coworkers. In writing, *completely* or *definitely* is safer.
examples: I **totally** forgot about your birthday; let me take you to lunch to make up for it.
"That movie was way too long." "**Totally**. I almost fell asleep."
The new version of the app looks **totally** different from the old one.

drill.sentence: "We should leave early to beat the traffic." "Oh, {{totally}}, let's head out at four."
drill.hint: yes, I fully agree (casual adverb; not *definitely*, *absolutely* or *for sure*)

entries.related: *completely* — neutral; *absolutely* — a strong yes, a bit more formal; *for sure* — a casual yes, very common.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something important or serious. *It's no big deal* or *It's not a big deal* means it doesn't matter or isn't a problem.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in speech and fine in casual work talk. The negative forms are the most common, often to calm someone down or to answer an apology. *Make a big deal (out) of something* means to make too much fuss about it.
entries.pattern: It's no big deal / not a big deal; make a big deal (out) of something
examples: Don't worry about the scratch on my car; it's **no big deal**.
Finishing college at fifty was **a big deal** for my mom, so the whole family flew in for it.
He forgot to call me back, but I'm not going to **make a big deal** out of it.

drill.sentence: "Sorry, I spilled coffee on your notebook." "Don't worry, it's not {{a big deal}}."
drill.hint: something important, three words (not *a problem* or *an issue*)

entries.related: *no biggie* — slangier form of *no big deal*; *a deal-breaker* — something that makes you say no to an offer; *serious* — the neutral adjective.

entries.label: quantifier
entries.meaning: A lot of; many or much. In casual American speech it works with both countable and uncountable nouns.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation and casual writing among all ages: *a bunch of people*, *a bunch of work*. *A whole bunch* is stronger, and *Thanks a bunch* means *thanks a lot*, sometimes sarcastically. In standard English *a bunch* is also a group of things held together, such as *a bunch of bananas*, which is not informal.
examples: We invited **a bunch of** people from the neighborhood, so I'll need way more chairs.
I spent **a bunch of** money on car repairs this month, so I'm skipping the concert.
There's **a whole bunch of** leftovers in the fridge if you're hungry.

drill.sentence: My cousin just got back from Japan and brought me {{a bunch of}} snacks I've never seen before.
drill.hint: a large number of, said casually (three words, US; not *a lot of*, *a ton of* or *lots of*)

entries.related: *a lot of* — neutral, works everywhere; *a ton of* / *tons of* — stronger, also casual; *a handful of* — only a few.

entries.label: filler word
entries.meaning: Used before a number or amount to mean *about* or *roughly*: *It took, like, an hour.*
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, especially among younger and middle-aged Americans, often with small pauses around it. It can sound careless, so avoid it in presentations, interviews and writing, where *about* or *around* is better. In this use it comes right before a number, a time or an amount.
examples: The line at the DMV was so long; I waited, **like**, two hours just to renew my license.
There were **like** fifty people at her birthday party, and I only knew three of them.
The concert's in, **like**, three hours, and I still haven't picked an outfit.

drill.sentence: The pizza place is close; it's {{like}} five minutes from here if you walk fast.
drill.hint: a casual spoken filler meaning *approximately* (not *about*, *around*, *roughly* or *maybe*)

entries.related: *about* / *around* — neutral, fine anywhere; *-ish* — added to a number (*sevenish*); *give or take* — after a number, means roughly.

entries.label: greeting
entries.meaning: A casual greeting that means *Hi, how are you, what's new?*
entries.usage: Common among friends, family and friendly coworkers, especially younger people, in speech and texts. The usual answer is *Not much* or *Nothing much*, often followed by *What's up with you?*; nobody expects a detailed answer. Said with a worried tone, as in *What's up, you look upset*, it means *what's wrong*.
examples: "Hey, **what's up**?" "Nothing much, just making dinner. What's up with you?"
**What's up**, man? I haven't seen you since the wedding.
I texted my sister "**what's up**" and she sent back twenty photos of her new puppy.

drill.sentence: Tyler walked into the kitchen, grabbed a soda and said, "{{What's up}}, everybody?"
drill.hint: a relaxed hello, two words (not *hey there*)

entries.related: *How's it going?* — similar, usually answered with *good*; *What's new?* — asks for news; *sup* — slang short form, mostly in texts.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be OK with something and not mind it. *Are you cool with that?* asks whether someone agrees with a plan.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech and texts, and fine with coworkers you know well. It is used about plans, changes and requests, often as a question to check that someone agrees. *We're cool* means there is no problem between two people after a disagreement.
examples: I'm thinking Thai food tonight, if you're **cool with** that.
My roommate said she's **cool with** me getting a cat as long as it stays out of her room.
Is everyone **cool with** moving the meeting to Thursday morning?

drill.sentence: I have to bring my little brother along tonight; I hope you're {{cool with}} that.
drill.hint: don't mind, casual US (not *fine with* or *okay with*)

entries.related: *be OK / fine with something* — neutral; *not mind* — polite, works everywhere; *be down for something* — slang, happy to join.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Disgusting; very unpleasant to see, smell, taste or touch.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech among all ages, often alone as a reaction: *Ew, gross!* It is mostly about food, smells, dirt and the body, but it can also describe behavior you find distasteful. In formal English *gross* means *total, before deductions* (*gross income*) or *very serious* (*gross negligence*), which is a separate sense.
examples: There's mold on this bread. **Gross**, how long has it been in here?
The gym locker room was so **gross** that I showered at home instead.
My kids think it's **gross** when my husband and I kiss in the kitchen.

drill.sentence: Someone left a half-eaten burrito under the seat on the bus, and it smelled so {{gross}}.
drill.hint: unpleasant enough to make you feel sick (casual US; not *bad*, *nasty* or *disgusting*)

entries.related: *disgusting* — neutral, stronger; *nasty* — similar, can also mean mean or cruel; *ew* — the sound people make, often before *gross*.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something annoying that takes extra time or effort, or causes small problems.
entries.usage: Common in speech and casual emails for all ages, and fine at work. Typical patterns are *It's a (real) hassle to* + verb, *not worth the hassle* and *hassle-free* (common in ads). As a verb, *hassle someone* means to keep bothering them.
entries.pattern: It's a hassle to + verb; not worth the hassle
examples: Renewing my passport was **a hassle**; I had to go to the post office three times.
Finding parking downtown is such **a hassle** that I just take the bus.
We thought about returning the couch, but honestly, it wasn't worth **the hassle**.

drill.sentence: Switching phone companies is {{a hassle}}, so I've been paying too much for years.
drill.hint: annoying and too much trouble, a noun (not *a pain*, *a headache* or *a chore*)

entries.related: *a pain* — similar, more casual; *a headache* — a problem that causes worry; *trouble* — neutral (*It's no trouble*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Having no money, or almost none, at the moment.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech among all ages, often with *totally* or *flat*: *I'm flat broke.* It usually describes a temporary situation (*broke until payday*) and sounds light, so it's not the word for real poverty. *Go broke* means a person or business loses all its money.
examples: I can't go out this weekend; I'm totally **broke** until I get paid on Friday.
We were so **broke** in college that we ate instant noodles every night.
The restaurant **went broke** after the new mall opened across town.

drill.sentence: After paying rent and my car insurance, I'm {{broke}} until the end of the month.
drill.hint: with no money left (one word, casual; not *poor*)

entries.related: *short on cash* — has little money, milder; *strapped (for cash)* — similar, informal; *skint* — the British equivalent; *bankrupt* — the formal, legal term.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To leave a place, or to set off on a trip, especially by car.
entries.usage: Casual and used by all ages: *We should hit the road before traffic gets bad.* It often signals that it's time to go home after a visit (*Well, I'd better hit the road*). As a command to another person, *Hit the road!* is a rude way to say *go away*.
examples: It's getting late and I've got a two-hour drive, so I'd better **hit the road**.
We packed the car the night before and **hit the road** at five in the morning.
After their album came out, the band **hit the road** for a six-month tour.

drill.sentence: If we want to reach the cabin before dark, we need to {{hit the road}} by noon.
drill.hint: start driving (idiom; not *get going*, *head out* or *leave*)

entries.related: *head out* — leave, very common; *get going* — leave or start, casual; *take off* — leave, often quickly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have a really fun, exciting time.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and texts about parties, trips, concerts and games. It is often in the past (*We had a blast*) or a wish before someone goes out (*Have a blast!*). *It was a blast* means the event was a lot of fun.
examples: We **had a blast** at the water park; the kids want to go back next weekend.
"I'm heading to the concert now." "Nice, **have a blast**!"
Thanks for inviting us to your housewarming; we **had an absolute blast**.

drill.sentence: Everyone danced until midnight at the wedding, and we {{had a blast}}.
drill.hint: enjoyed ourselves a lot (not *had a great time*, *had fun* or *had a ball*)

entries.related: *have a great time* — neutral; *have a ball* — similar, a bit old-fashioned; *a blast from the past* — something that reminds you of earlier times.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Unnecessary conflict, gossip and emotional fuss between people, for example in a friend group, a family or a workplace.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, especially among younger adults: *I don't want any drama.* It is critical and suggests people create problems out of habit or for attention. Common patterns are *so much drama*, *family drama*, *work drama*, and *a drama queen* for a person who overreacts.
examples: There's always some **drama** in my friend group, so I mostly stay out of the group chat.
I'm skipping my cousin's wedding; there's too much family **drama**.
She left her old job because of all the office **drama**, not because of the pay.

drill.sentence: Every time Tina and Jess are in the same room there's {{drama}}, so I invite them on different nights.
drill.hint: emotional fuss and conflict (not *tension* or *trouble*)

entries.related: *a drama queen* — a person who overreacts; *a scene* — a loud emotional display in public; *beef* — slang, an ongoing conflict between two people.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Strange or unpleasant in a way that makes you feel uneasy or a little afraid.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages. It describes places, sounds and stories (*a creepy old house*) and also people whose behavior feels wrong, especially unwanted attention. Said about a person it is strong criticism; *a creep* is a person who acts this way.
examples: The basement is really **creepy** at night, so I always leave the light on.
Some guy at the bar kept staring at us, and it was kind of **creepy**.
It's a little **creepy** how my phone shows me ads for things I only talked about.

drill.sentence: The old doll's eyes seemed to follow you around the room, which was honestly {{creepy}}.
drill.hint: making you uneasy and a little scared (not *scary*, *spooky* or *weird*)

entries.related: *scary* — frightening, more direct; *spooky* — eerie, often lighter, like a ghost story; *weird* — just strange, not necessarily uncomfortable.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is rude, mean or selfish; a mild insult.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech among all ages, mild enough for TV and for use around kids, but still an insult. It often describes one action (*Don't be a jerk*), and people use it when apologizing for their own behavior (*I was a jerk*). British speakers more often say *idiot*, *git* or *prat*.
examples: He cut in front of everyone in line and then yelled at the cashier. What **a jerk**.
I'm sorry I was **a jerk** at dinner; I shouldn't have made fun of your haircut.
Don't be **a jerk**; let your little sister play too.

drill.sentence: My neighbor keeps parking in my spot and laughs when I complain; he's such {{a jerk}}.
drill.hint: a rude, selfish person (mild US insult; not *an idiot* or *a pain*)

entries.related: *an idiot* — stupid rather than mean; *a creep* — someone who makes others uneasy; *rude* — the neutral adjective.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A friend. *Buddy* is also a friendly way to address a man or a boy, often one you don't know well.
entries.usage: Common in American speech, mostly among men or when talking to boys (*Hey buddy, are you lost?*). Said to an adult stranger in an annoyed tone, it sounds unfriendly (*Listen, buddy…*). Compounds are neutral and used by everyone: *a workout buddy*, *a study buddy*.
examples: I'm going fishing with a couple of my old college **buddies** this weekend.
Hey **buddy**, did you lose your mom? Let's go find her.
My gym **buddy** texts me at six every morning, so I can't skip workouts.

drill.sentence: My {{buddy}} Dave has a pickup truck, so he's helping me move on Saturday.
drill.hint: a male friend, casual US word (not *friend*, *pal* or *bro*)

entries.related: *pal* — similar, a bit dated; *bro* — slang, mostly younger men; *dude* — casual address, mostly to men.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To end a romantic relationship with someone, often suddenly or without much kindness.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech for all ages: *She dumped him after two months.* It is blunt, and people often use it in the passive about themselves (*I got dumped*). *Break up with someone* is the neutral, kinder way to say it.
examples: Tom's been really quiet since his girlfriend **dumped** him last month.
I can't believe he **dumped** her by text after three years together.
I **got dumped** right before Valentine's Day, so I spent it eating pizza with my sister.

drill.sentence: After six months of dating, Kayla {{dumped}} her boyfriend because he never made time for her.
drill.hint: ended things with, bluntly (not *left*, *ditched* or *broke up with*)

entries.related: *break up with someone* — neutral; *split up* — both people end it; *ghost someone* — disappear without explanation.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A former boyfriend, girlfriend, husband or wife.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and casual writing, and fine almost anywhere except formal documents. It usually comes with a possessive: *my ex*, *her ex*. *Ex-* is also a prefix (*ex-wife*, *ex-boss*), but *an ex* on its own almost always means a former partner.
examples: I ran into my **ex** at the grocery store, and it was super awkward.
She's still friends with her **ex**, and they share the dog.
He kept talking about his **ex** on our first date, which wasn't a great sign.

drill.sentence: We broke up three years ago, but my {{ex}} still sends me a text on my birthday.
drill.hint: former partner, a two-letter noun

entries.related: *ex-husband* / *ex-girlfriend* — more specific; *former partner* — neutral, more formal; *an old flame* — a past love, a bit old-fashioned.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To feel romantically attracted to someone, usually secretly and often without any relationship.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, especially about teenagers, coworkers and celebrities. It suggests a light, often short-lived feeling that the other person may not know about. Patterns: *have a (huge) crush on someone*, *my crush* (= the person I like), *my high school crush*.
examples: In middle school I **had a crush on** a boy in my Spanish class but never said a word to him.
I think Mia **has a crush on** the new guy in accounting; she keeps finding reasons to visit his desk.
My daughter **has a crush on** someone from her soccer team, and she's too embarrassed to talk about it.

drill.sentence: My roommate blushes every time the barista says hi; I'm pretty sure she {{has a crush on}} him.
drill.hint: is secretly attracted to (not *likes*, *is into* or *has a thing for*)

entries.related: *have a thing for someone* — similar, casual; *be into someone* — attracted, casual; *fall for someone* — start to love someone.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To want to do something very much and feel impatient to do it.
entries.usage: A common exaggeration in casual speech and friendly emails: *I'm dying to see it.* It is always in the progressive (*I'm dying to*, *She was dying to*) and takes *to* + verb, or *for* + noun (*dying for a coffee*). It sounds enthusiastic and is fine with friends and coworkers.
entries.pattern: be dying to + verb / be dying for + noun
examples: I've heard so much about that new ramen place; I'm **dying to** try it.
My parents are **dying to** meet you, so please come to dinner on Sunday.
After a week of hospital food, he was **dying for** a real burger.

drill.sentence: She's been talking about Iceland for years, and she's {{dying to}} see the northern lights.
drill.hint: wants very much, impatiently (not *eager to*, *desperate to*, *itching to* or *longing to*)

entries.related: *can't wait to* — very common, similar meaning; *be desperate to* — stronger, more negative; *be itching to* — eager to start something.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To cause someone a lot of pain or discomfort; said about a body part that hurts, or a thing that makes it hurt.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, almost always in the progressive and usually with *me*: *My back is killing me.* It is an exaggeration for pain or discomfort, not danger. *You're killing me* is a different, joking use that means *you're so funny* or *you're driving me crazy*.
entries.pattern: my feet / back / head + be killing me
examples: We walked all over the city today, and my feet are **killing me**.
These new boots look great, but they're **killing me**.
My back's been **killing me** since I helped my brother move his couch.

drill.sentence: Can we sit down for a minute? My knees are {{killing me}} after all those stairs.
drill.hint: causing me a lot of pain (an exaggeration)

entries.related: *hurt* — neutral (*My feet hurt*); *ache* — a dull, lasting pain; *be sore* — hurt after exercise or an injury.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: In casual use, to love something a lot and think about it all the time; a happy exaggeration.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, texts and social media, especially among younger people: *I'm obsessed with this song.* It is usually positive and playful, about food, shows, songs, products or pets. The literal sense, an unhealthy fixation (*obsessed with his weight*), is serious, so context decides.
examples: I'm **obsessed with** this new coffee shop; I've been there every morning this week.
My niece is **obsessed with** dinosaurs and knows the names of about fifty of them.
We watched the whole season in two days; we're totally **obsessed**.

drill.sentence: My dad is {{obsessed with}} his new air fryer; he's made fries, chicken and even cake in it.
drill.hint: loves it and thinks about it all the time (not *crazy about*, *hooked on* or *into*)

entries.related: *be into something* — like something, weaker; *be hooked on something* — can't stop, often a show or game; *be crazy about something* — very enthusiastic.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very hungry; an everyday exaggeration, not real starvation.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech: *I'm starving, let's eat.* It is an exaggeration for a missed lunch or a long day; in news and serious contexts *starving* means really suffering from lack of food. *I'm starved* means the same and is common in American speech.
examples: I skipped breakfast and lunch, so I'm **starving**. Can we eat now?
The kids came home from swim practice **starving** and finished a whole pizza in ten minutes.
Don't go grocery shopping when you're **starving**; you'll buy way too much junk food.

drill.sentence: "Want to grab dinner?" "Yes, please. I'm {{starving}}; all I've had today is a granola bar."
drill.hint: extremely hungry, an exaggeration (-ing form; not *famished* or *hungry*)

entries.related: *famished* — the same, a bit more formal or playful; *peckish* — a little hungry, British; *stuffed* — the opposite, completely full.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Completely full after eating, often uncomfortably full.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, usually after a big meal: *I'm stuffed.* It is also a friendly way to say no to more food at someone's home (*No thanks, I'm stuffed*). In cooking, *stuffed* means filled with something (*stuffed peppers*), which is a neutral, separate sense.
examples: I can't eat another bite; I'm completely **stuffed**.
After Thanksgiving dinner, we were all so **stuffed** that we fell asleep on the couch.
"Want some pie?" "Thanks, but I'm **stuffed**."

drill.sentence: That burger was huge; I'm so {{stuffed}} I don't think I'll eat dinner tonight.
drill.hint: completely full of food (not *full*)

entries.related: *full* — neutral; *I couldn't eat another bite* — polite and a bit more formal; *starving* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To want a particular food or drink very strongly, often suddenly.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech: *I'm craving pizza.* For a wish you have right now it is usually progressive, and the verb takes a direct object; *for* goes after the noun (*a craving for pizza*). Typical topics are pregnancy, diets and late-night snacks, and more seriously cigarettes or drugs.
examples: I've been **craving** tacos all day, so let's go to that place on Fifth Street.
When she was pregnant, my sister **craved** spicy food and nothing else.
By the end of our trip to Japan, I was **craving** a plain old cheeseburger.

drill.sentence: It's eleven at night and I'm {{craving}} something sweet. Do we have any cookies left?
drill.hint: strongly and suddenly want (a food) (not *dying for* or *in the mood for*)

mistake.why: In everyday speech *crave* takes a direct object; *for* goes after the noun: *a craving for tacos*.

entries.related: *a craving (for something)* — the noun; *be in the mood for something* — milder; *be dying for something* — a stronger exaggeration.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To take a very long time, usually longer than you want.
entries.usage: A common exaggeration in casual speech and texts for all ages, often showing impatience: *This line is taking forever.* Typical patterns are *It took forever* and *It took forever to* + verb. British speakers more often say *take ages*.
examples: The pasta **took forever** to cook because our stove is so old.
Sorry I'm late; the bus **took forever**.
It's **taking forever** to hear back about the apartment, and I'm getting nervous.

drill.sentence: Let's take the highway; the back roads always {{take forever}} on a Friday afternoon.
drill.hint: need an extremely long time (US, two words; the British version ends in *ages*)

entries.related: *take ages* — the same, more British; *take a while* — neutral and weaker; *drag on* — continue too long, about events.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be doing or planning something, as in *What are you up to tonight?* With a suspicious tone, *up to something* means doing something secret or naughty.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texts: *What are you up to this weekend?* is a friendly way to ask about plans, and *Not much* is a normal answer. *What have you been up to?* asks what someone has done recently, often after a long time apart. Don't confuse it with *It's up to you* (= your decision).
examples: Hey, what are you **up to** tonight? Want to grab dinner?
I haven't seen you in months; what have you been **up to**?
My cat keeps sneaking behind the couch; I think she's **up to** something.

drill.sentence: "What are you {{up to}} this weekend?" "Not much, just laundry and football on TV."
drill.hint: doing or planning, two short words (not *doing*)

entries.related: *be up for something* — be willing to do it; *be into something* — be interested in it; *be up to someone* — be their decision.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To manage to get somewhere in time, or to manage to come to an event; also to become successful in a career.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and casual emails for arriving after a rush (*We made it*) and for coming to an event (*Can you make it on Friday?*). *Sorry, I can't make it* is a polite way to decline an invitation. The career sense often appears as *make it big* or *make it in* + place or field (*make it in Hollywood*).
examples: We ran through the airport and **made it** to the gate just before they closed the doors.
Sorry, I can't **make it** to your party on Saturday; I'm working a double shift.
Thousands of actors move to Los Angeles every year, but only a few **make it**.

drill.sentence: The traffic was terrible, but we {{made it}} to the theater five minutes before the show started.
drill.hint: managed to arrive in time (two words; not *got*)

entries.related: *make it big* — become very successful; *pull it off* — succeed at something hard; *show up* — arrive, without the idea of difficulty.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Ready to start or leave, with everything prepared, checked or approved.
entries.usage: Common in American speech and casual work emails, often said by someone who has just checked or prepared something for you, like a mechanic, a nurse or a coworker: *You're good to go.* It also works as a question to check that everyone is ready: *Are we good to go?*
examples: Your tires have been rotated and the oil's changed, so you're **good to go**.
After a quick look at my stitches, the doctor said I was **good to go**.
I've packed the cooler and filled the tank; are we **good to go**?

drill.sentence: The vet says the dog's leg has healed, so she's {{good to go}} for long walks again.
drill.hint: ready, with nothing left to fix (three words; not *all set* or *ready to go*)

entries.related: *all set* — the same meaning, very common; *ready to roll* — casual, ready to start; *a go* — approved (*The trip is a go*).

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A warm, casual way to thank someone, meaning *thank you so much, you're wonderful*.
entries.usage: Common in American speech and texts with friends, family and friendly coworkers, usually right after someone does you a favor: *Thanks, you're the best!* It is not a real ranking; it just shows strong thanks. It's too familiar for an email to someone you don't know well.
examples: You picked up my dry cleaning? Thank you, **you're the best**!
"I saved you a seat in the front row." "Aw, **you're the best**."
Mom, thanks for watching the kids on such short notice; **you're the best**.

drill.sentence: You brought me soup when I was sick? Seriously, {{you're the best}}.
drill.hint: warm thanks, three words ending in a superlative (not *you rock*)

entries.related: *you rock* — similar, slangier; *you're a lifesaver* — thanks for help in a difficult moment; *I owe you one* — I'll return the favor.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: An annoyed reply that means *stop it, be fair to me*, or *I don't believe that, it's ridiculous*.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages; it sounds irritated or mocking, so be careful with people you don't know well. It answers unfair criticism (*Give me a break, it's my first day!*) or a claim you find ridiculous. In fast speech it sounds like *gimme a break*.
examples: Oh, **give me a break**, I was only five minutes late.
He claims the dog ate his car keys? **Give me a break**.
**Give me a break**, Mom! I cleaned my room yesterday.

drill.sentence: He says he's too busy to call, but he posts photos every hour? {{Give me a break}}.
drill.hint: I don't believe that for a second (four words; not *come on* or *please*)

entries.related: *come on* — a milder protest; *yeah, right* — sarcastic disbelief; *take a break* — rest for a short time, a different phrase.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *It doesn't matter, don't bother*; also a firm *absolutely not* in reply to a request.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages. *Never mind, forget it* drops a topic or a request, sometimes with a little annoyance if you feel nobody is listening. As a reply to a request, *Forget it!* is a blunt refusal, so it can sound rude.
examples: "What were you going to say?" "Oh, **forget it**, it's not important."
"Can I borrow your car for the weekend?" "**Forget it**. You still haven't fixed the dent from last time."
I tried to explain the rules twice, then said **forget it** and we watched a movie instead.

drill.sentence: "Wait, what did you just say?" "Never mind, {{forget it}}; it wasn't that funny anyway."
drill.hint: it doesn't matter, don't bother (two words; not *skip it* or *drop it*)

entries.related: *never mind* — the same idea, softer; *no way* — a casual refusal; *forget about it* — also a casual reply to thanks (*don't mention it*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To understand something, such as an explanation, a joke or someone's feelings.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech for all ages and fine at work: *I don't get it.* It is used for jokes (*Did you get the joke?*), explanations and other people's reactions (*I get why you're upset*). *I get it* can also sound impatient, meaning *I understand, you don't need to repeat it*.
entries.pattern: get it / get + the joke / get why …
examples: I read the instructions three times, and I still don't **get it**.
Everyone laughed at the joke, but I didn't **get it** until later.
I **get** why you're upset; I'd be mad too if he canceled on me.

drill.sentence: Okay, okay, I {{get it}}; you don't have to explain it again.
drill.hint: understand you, two short words (present tense; not *got it*)

entries.related: *got it* — a quick reply meaning *understood*; *figure out* — understand after thinking; *get the picture* — understand a situation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go to the gym to work out. In the same way, *hit* + a place means go there: *hit the beach*, *hit the mall*.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and social media: *I'm going to hit the gym after work.* *Hit* + place suggests energy or a planned trip: *hit the beach*, *hit the stores*, *hit the books* (= study hard). It's too casual for writing, where *go to the gym* or *work out* is better.
examples: I try to **hit the gym** before work, so I'm usually in bed by ten.
As soon as we got to the hotel, we changed and **hit the beach**.
We're going to **hit the outlet mall** on Saturday to look for a new winter coat.

drill.sentence: I've been sitting at my desk all day, so I'm going to {{hit the gym}} for an hour.
drill.hint: go exercise, casual US (three words; not *work out*)

entries.related: *hit the books* — study hard; *hit the sack* / *hit the hay* — go to bed; *work out* — exercise, neutral.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: In casual speech: extreme, shocking or amazing, as in *The traffic was insane.*
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech among younger and middle-aged speakers; it can be negative (*insane prices*) or very positive (*an insane goal*). It also works as an intensifier: *insanely good*. Avoid it in formal writing, and don't use it about mental illness, where it sounds offensive and outdated.
examples: The traffic on the way to the airport was **insane**; it took us two hours to go ten miles.
Did you see that catch in the fourth quarter? It was **insane**.
Rent in this neighborhood is **insane**; a tiny studio costs three thousand a month.

drill.sentence: There were so many people at the Black Friday sale that the lines were {{insane}}.
drill.hint: unbelievably extreme (casual; not *crazy*, *nuts*, *wild* or *ridiculous*)

entries.related: *crazy* — very similar, also casual; *wild* — surprising rather than extreme; *ridiculous* — extreme in an unreasonable way.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Amazing, strange or hard to believe, as in *That's wild.*
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech and texts, especially as a reaction to a surprising story: *That's wild*, *That's so wild*. It shows surprise or amazement, not approval or disapproval. Fine with friends and coworkers, but not in formal writing.
examples: You ran into your high school teacher in Tokyo? That's **wild**.
It's **wild** how fast my nephew is growing; he's taller than me now.
The end of the game was **wild**, with three goals in the last five minutes.

drill.sentence: "My new boss went to high school with my dad." "No way, that's {{wild}}!"
drill.hint: hard to believe (one word, casual US; not *crazy*, *insane*, *nuts* or *amazing*)

entries.related: *crazy* / *insane* — similar, stronger; *no way* — a reaction of disbelief; *wild* in *wild animals* — not tame, a standard sense.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be finished with something; also to be fed up and want nothing more to do with something or someone.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech: *Are you done with the salt?*, *I'm done for the day.* With emphasis (*I'm done!*, *I'm so done with this*), it means you've had enough and are quitting or ending a relationship. Some traditional style guides prefer *finished* for people, but *done* is normal in everyday American English.
examples: Are you **done with** the laptop? I need to check my email.
He lied to me again. I'm **done**; I'm not answering his calls anymore.
Once you're **done with** your homework, you can go to Leo's house.

drill.sentence: This is the third time the restaurant got my order wrong; I'm {{done with}} that place.
drill.hint: fed up and never going back to (not *sick of*, *over* or *through with*)

entries.related: *finished* — neutral; *be fed up (with something)* — annoyed and out of patience; *be over something* — no longer care about it, slang.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Relaxed and easygoing; not easily worried or upset, and not strict.
entries.usage: Used by all ages about people, places and styles: *a laid-back boss*, *a laid-back beach town*. It is positive or neutral and fine in conversation and casual work talk. It is hyphenated before a noun; after a verb you see both *laid-back* and *laid back*.
examples: My new boss is pretty **laid-back**; she doesn't care when we come in as long as the work gets done.
We loved the **laid-back** feel of the little beach town.
My parents were really **laid-back** about curfews when I was a teenager.

drill.sentence: Our yoga teacher is so {{laid-back}} that she doesn't mind when people show up ten minutes late.
drill.hint: calm and never stressed (hyphenated; not *chill*, *relaxed* or *easygoing*)

entries.related: *easygoing* — very similar, about personality; *chill* — slang, relaxed; *uptight* — the opposite, tense and strict.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Wrong, unfair or disturbing, as in *That's so messed up.* It can also mean emotionally damaged or in a bad state.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech, especially among younger adults, as a reaction to unfair or cruel behavior. It is mild enough for friends and most coworkers, though not for formal writing. The verb *mess up* means *make a mistake* (*I messed up*), a related but different use.
examples: They fired her the day after she came back from maternity leave? That's so **messed up**.
It's really **messed up** that he told everyone your secret after he promised not to.
He's been kind of **messed up** since the accident, so go easy on him.

drill.sentence: Charging people a fee just to cancel their account is really {{messed up}}.
drill.hint: morally wrong and upsetting (casual US, two words; not *unfair* or *shady*)

entries.related: *not cool* — milder disapproval; *twisted* — disturbing in a sick or cruel way; *mess up* (verb) — make a mistake.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Possible to do; realistic, though maybe not easy.
entries.usage: Common in speech and casual work talk for all ages, often about deadlines, plans and workouts: *Two weeks is tight, but it's doable.* It usually suggests that effort is needed, so it sounds reassuring after a challenge is described. In formal writing, *feasible* or *achievable* is more usual.
examples: Running a half marathon in the spring is **doable** if you start training now.
Moving the whole family across the country in a week? It's tight, but it's **doable**.
The client wants the new logo by Friday, which is **doable** if nobody gets sick.

drill.sentence: The hike is long, but with a few breaks it's definitely {{doable}} for the kids.
drill.hint: can be managed without too much trouble (one word; not *possible* or *manageable*)

entries.related: *feasible* — formal, often in planning; *manageable* — not too hard to handle; *a stretch* — possible but difficult.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very crowded; completely full of people.
entries.usage: Common in speech and casual writing for all ages, about places and events: *The bar was packed*, *a packed stadium*. *Packed with* + noun means full of something (*packed with tourists*), and *jam-packed* is even stronger. A *packed schedule* is one with no free time.
examples: The subway was so **packed** this morning that I couldn't even reach the pole.
We tried the new brunch place, but it was **packed**, so we got bagels instead.
The stadium was **packed** for the last game of the season.

drill.sentence: Get there early; the farmers market is always {{packed}} on Saturday mornings.
drill.hint: full of people (one word; not *crowded*, *busy* or *mobbed*)

entries.related: *crowded* — neutral; *jam-packed* — even more full; *dead* — informal opposite, almost empty.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who feels best, most awake and most active early in the day.
entries.usage: Used by all ages, very often in the negative: *I'm not a morning person* is a light, common way to explain being slow or grumpy before noon. The opposite is *a night person* or *a night owl*. It's casual but fine at work.
examples: My husband is **a morning person**; he's out running at six while I'm still asleep.
Don't talk to me before my coffee; I'm not **a morning person**.
If you're **a morning person**, the early shift at the bakery will suit you.

drill.sentence: My roommate sings in the shower at six a.m.; she's definitely {{a morning person}}.
drill.hint: someone who loves the early hours (three words; not *an early bird*)

entries.related: *an early bird* — someone who gets up early; *a night owl* — someone who stays up late and is most active at night.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To not come to a date or meeting with someone, without telling them.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, especially about dates: *I got stood up.* The object normally goes between *stand* and *up* (*She stood me up*), and the passive with *get* is very common. It is critical, since the other person was left waiting.
entries.pattern: stand someone up / get stood up
examples: Her blind date **stood her up**, so she ate dessert alone and went home.
She **got stood up** on her first date in years, so we took her out for drinks instead.
The plumber **stood us up** twice, so we finally called another company.

drill.sentence: We had a date at seven, but she never came or texted; she {{stood me up}}.
drill.hint: didn't come to meet me, without warning (not *ghosted me*, *bailed on me* or *flaked on me*)

entries.related: *bail on someone* — cancel at the last minute; *ghost someone* — stop answering completely; *a no-show* — a person who doesn't come.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A police officer.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, TV and news headlines, and used by all ages; it is informal but not rude. In formal writing, and when speaking to an officer, say *police officer* or *officer* (*Excuse me, officer*). *The cops* means the police in general (*Call the cops!*).
examples: A **cop** stopped me on the way home because one of my taillights was out.
Our neighbors were so loud that someone finally called the **cops**.
My uncle was a **cop** in Chicago for twenty years before he retired.

drill.sentence: There was an accident on Main Street, and two {{cops}} were directing traffic around it.
drill.hint: police officers (casual, plural; not *officers*)

entries.related: *police officer* — neutral and formal; *officer* — the polite form of address; *the police* — the institution.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Bad-tempered and easily annoyed, often because you are tired, hungry or unwell.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech about kids, older people, and adults who haven't slept or eaten: *He gets cranky when he's hungry.* It sounds light and a bit affectionate, not like serious criticism. In British English *cranky* can also mean *strange* or *eccentric*.
examples: The baby skipped her nap, so she's been **cranky** all afternoon.
I've been **cranky** all week because the neighbors' dog keeps waking me up at five.
My husband gets a little **cranky** when the TV remote goes missing.

drill.sentence: We'd better stop for lunch soon; the kids get really {{cranky}} when they're hungry.
drill.hint: bad-tempered (US; not *grumpy*, *moody* or *hangry*)

entries.related: *grumpy* — very similar, common in British English too; *hangry* — slang, irritable because hungry; *irritable* — neutral.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A mild form of *what the hell*: it shows surprise or annoyance, and *Oh, what the heck* also means *why not?* before a sudden decision.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech for all ages; *heck* is a polite substitute for *hell*, so it's fine around kids and most coworkers. *What the heck is that?* shows surprise or annoyance, while *What the heck, let's do it* shows a sudden decision. It sounds mild and a little wholesome.
examples: **What the heck** did you put in this chili? It's amazing.
I wasn't going to order dessert, but **what the heck**, it's my birthday.
**What the heck**? Someone parked right behind me and blocked me in.

drill.sentence: I said I'd never try karaoke, but {{what the heck}}, let's sing one song.
drill.hint: why not, said mildly (three words; not *why not* or the stronger version with *hell*)

entries.related: *what the hell* — the same, ruder; *heck* — the mild word on its own (*a heck of a lot*); *why not?* — a neutral way to agree to try something.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Sexually attractive; very good-looking.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech among younger and middle-aged adults, mostly with friends: *He's so hot.* It is openly about physical attraction, so it's out of place at work and can sound rude if said to or about a stranger. *Attractive* and *good-looking* are neutral; *cute* is softer.
examples: Everyone at the wedding kept asking who the **hot** guy in the blue suit was.
Let's be honest: half the reason we watch that show is that the lead actor is so **hot**.
She showed me a photo of her new boyfriend, and wow, he's **hot**.

drill.sentence: Lena keeps going back to the bakery because she thinks the guy at the register is really {{hot}}.
drill.hint: physically very attractive (casual, one word; not *cute*, *handsome* or *sexy*)

entries.related: *cute* — attractive in a sweet or softer way; *good-looking* — neutral; *sexy* — more direct about sexual appeal.
